blurb: The Alaouite sultans and kings, from 1666 to today
dateConvention: Dates are Western (Gregorian); Moroccan chronicles use the Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar, and their dates are given as their standard Western equivalents. The rulers were sultans until Mohammed V took the title of king in 1957.

reigns.tagline: The desert prince who stitched Morocco back together
reigns.previously: The Saadians are gone. Morocco is carved up by lodges and warlords.
paragraphs: Back in 1591 Morocco's Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur crossed the Sahara, smashed the Songhay empire and came home dripping with gold. When he died in 1603 his sons tore the country apart. By the 1660s the last Saadians were gone, and Morocco was a patchwork: the powerful Sufi lodge of Dila in the Middle Atlas, local strongmen in the north, holy men in the south.

Out in the Tafilalt oasis lived a family of sharifs, who traced their line back to the Prophet. One son, al-Rashid, fell out with his brother Muhammad and went off to build his own following. In 1664 the brothers fought, and Muhammad was killed. Al-Rashid swept on: Taza, then Fez in 1666, where he was hailed as sultan. In 1668 he wiped out the Dila lodge, and Marrakesh fell soon after.

In about six years he had put the whole country back under one ruler. Then, in April 1672, in a garden in Marrakesh, his horse bolted and he smashed his head on the branch of an orange tree. He was about 41. Waiting in Fez as governor was his younger half-brother, Ismail.

claims.text: Al-Rashid got his start by robbing a rich Jewish merchant called Ibn Mash'al and using the loot to raise an army.
claims.note: A later tradition, kept alive by the Fez students' carnival of the 'sultan of the students'. Contemporary sources don't back it up.

claims.text: He died when his bolting horse threw him against an orange tree.
claims.note: This is the standard account, reported by people writing at the time.

claims.text: The Alaouites trace their descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan.
claims.note: Confirmed as the family's own claim, and the basis of its right to rule. It can't be checked independently.

reigns.hook: The sultan is dead after barely six years. His half-brother Ismail, governor of Fez, doesn't wait for anyone's permission. He moves fast.

images.caption: The courtyard of the Cherratine madrasa in Fez, the college al-Rashid founded in 1670. No portrait of him survives.
images.alt: View looking up from the main courtyard of the Cherratine madrasa in Fez

reigns.tagline: Fifty-five years, a slave army and a city of walls
reigns.previously: Al-Rashid dies in a riding accident after reuniting Morocco.
paragraphs: Moulay Ismail was proclaimed in Fez days after his brother's death, then spent fifteen years fighting his nephew Ahmad ibn Muhriz for the throne. To make sure no one could do that again, he built an army that answered to him alone: the Black Guard, enslaved black soldiers raised from boyhood. Chroniclers put it at 150,000 men. He made Meknes his capital and built on a vast scale: palaces, huge granaries, stables, miles of walls and the great gate of Bab Mansour.

He went after the Europeans on his coast and took back Mehdya, Tangier (which the English gave up in 1684), Larache and Asilah. Spanish Ceuta held out against a siege that dragged on for decades. Corsairs from Salé brought in Christian captives by the thousand, and many were set to work on his building sites. One was a Cornish cabin boy, Thomas Pellow, taken in 1715, who spent 23 years as a captive in Morocco and later wrote it all down.
He reigned 55 years, longer than any other Moroccan sultan. When he died in 1727 he left a ruthless army and dozens of grown sons.

claims.text: Ismail fathered 888 children.
claims.note: The counts come from chroniclers and foreign visitors and vary. All that's safe to say is that he had more than 800 by a harem of hundreds of women.

claims.text: He asked Louis XIV for the hand of his daughter, the Princesse de Conti.
claims.note: French sources tell the story around the Moroccan embassy of 1699. Whether a formal proposal was ever made is unclear.

claims.text: He killed servants on a whim.
claims.note: Comes from European captives and envoys, who had every reason to paint him as a monster. Their tales can't be checked.

reigns.hook: The old lion is dead. The Black Guard move first and hail one of his sons, Ahmad, as sultan. But Ahmad is one of dozens, and the slave army that crowned him answers to no one.

images.caption: From the 1683 book of Germain Moüette, a Frenchman held captive in Morocco; how lifelike it is, nobody knows.
images.alt: Old European engraving of Moulay Ismail

reigns.tagline: Gold for the soldiers, and a throne that lasted a year
reigns.previously: Moulay Ismail dies after 55 years, leaving dozens of sons.
paragraphs: When Moulay Ismail died in March 1727, the Black Guard moved before anyone else could. At Meknes they hailed one of his sons, Ahmad, a man of about 50 who had once governed the Tadla region for his father. He opened the treasury and handed out coin to the soldiers by the fistful. That, so the story goes, is how he got his nickname: adh-Dhahabi, "the Golden".

Buying the army was easy. Keeping it was harder. The chroniclers paint him as weak and fond of drink, a sultan who let others run things while the money drained away. Within a year he had lost his grip. In March 1728 he was overthrown, and his half-brother Abd al-Malik was proclaimed in his place.

claims.text: He was called "the Golden" because he showered the soldiers with gold.
claims.note: This is the usual explanation in the Moroccan chronicles, and it fits an army that had just picked him. Nobody recorded where the name really came from.

claims.text: Ahmad was a drunkard who could not rule.
claims.note: The charge comes from later Moroccan chroniclers and from John Braithwaite, an Englishman in Morocco in 1727 and 1728. Both were writing about a loser, and neither was kind to him.

claims.text: His own wives were behind the coup that toppled him.
claims.note: One modern account says his wives started the plot once his drinking became public; others give the Black Guard the lead. The sources for these years are thin.

reigns.hook: Abd al-Malik has the throne. But he has a sharp tongue, the Black Guard are listening, and his brother Ahmad is still out there.

reigns.tagline: He picked a fight with the army that made him
reigns.previously: Ahmad the Golden, weak and fond of drink, is overthrown.
paragraphs: Abd al-Malik had once been lined up as Ismail's heir, until he fell out of favour and Ahmad was preferred. In March 1728 he got his chance, and he wasted it fast. He let Ahmad slip away. Then he tried to rein in the Black Guard and criticised them openly. The soldiers simply switched sides and went back to Ahmad.

Bloody fighting followed, and the brothers ended up splitting Morocco between them: Ahmad at Meknes, Abd al-Malik at Fez. It did not last. By July 1728 Abd al-Malik had lost his throne. He tried one last trick, a face-to-face meeting with Ahmad at which he meant to kill him. It failed. He was taken to Meknes under guard and locked up in a house there.

claims.text: Abd al-Malik lost the throne because he insulted the Black Guard.
claims.note: The story comes from John Braithwaite, an Englishman in Morocco at the time, and from later Moroccan chronicles. With so few sources, the soldiers' real reasons are hard to pin down.

claims.text: He was strangled in prison in Meknes on the night of 2 March 1729.
claims.note: Given by the chronicler al-Nasiri and by the historian Chouki El Hamel.

claims.text: He was born in 1675.
claims.note: His biography gives 1675, which would make him the elder brother. One list of rulers gives 1696 instead. Nobody has settled it.

reigns.hook: Ahmad the Golden is sultan again in Meknes, and the brother who tried to kill him is his prisoner. Only one of them can come out of this alive. As it turns out, neither will.

reigns.tagline: Restored, then dead three days after his brother
reigns.previously: Abd al-Malik's plot to kill Ahmad fails, and he ends up a prisoner.
paragraphs: Ahmad had been thrown out in the spring. By the summer the Black Guard had brought him back. In July 1728 he was sultan again in Meknes, and this time he had a score to settle. His brother Abd al-Malik had tried to have him murdered. Now Abd al-Malik sat under guard in a house in Meknes, waiting to find out what Ahmad would do with him.

In his short time on the throne Ahmad also enlarged the mausoleum where his father lay. On the night of 2 March 1729 Abd al-Malik was strangled in his prison. Three days later, on 5 March, Ahmad himself was dead. He was buried in that same mausoleum, next to Ismail. Two sultans were gone in a week, and the Black Guard went looking for the next son.

claims.text: Ahmad ordered his brother's murder.
claims.note: The killing happened in Ahmad's prison while he held the throne, and it is usually laid at his door. No surviving account records him giving the order.

claims.text: Ahmad died of an illness.
claims.note: Illness is the usual account of his death, but the sources say very little about it.

claims.text: He is buried beside his father in the Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail.
claims.note: His marble tombstone is in the tomb chamber at Meknes, next to Ismail's. Histories of the building also credit him with enlarging it.

reigns.hook: Two sons of Ismail are dead in a week. The army and the scholars of Fez agree on a third, Abdallah, and send riders south to fetch him. His mother is a force in her own right.

images.caption: The tomb chamber of the Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail in Meknes, where Ahmad was buried beside his father.

reigns.tagline: Round one for the sultan who always came back
reigns.cameToPower: Fetched from Sijilmasa by the army
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed; fled to the far south
reigns.previously: Abd al-Malik is strangled in prison; Ahmad dies three days later.
paragraphs: With two brothers dead in a week, the Black Guard, the Udaya troops and the army chiefs settled on Abdallah, about 35 and living in Sijilmasa, and the scholars of Fez gave their pledge too. His mother was Khanatha bint Bakkar, a chief's daughter from the far south. She was a learned woman who had advised Ismail himself, and she would stand behind her son for the next 25 years.

Abdallah finished his father's great gate at Meknes, Bab Mansour, in 1732, and built himself a fortified palace at Fez, Dar Dbibegh. His rule was harsh, with heavy demands on Fez and the tribes, and the soldiers soon soured on him. In September 1734 the Black Guard plotted to depose and kill him. He got wind of it and fled south to his mother's people at Oued Noun, taking his sons with him.

claims.text: His mother Khanatha bint Bakkar steered him through his many comebacks.
claims.note: Confirmed in outline: she was an influential widow of Ismail and a scholar. How much she directed events is a matter of interpretation.

claims.text: Abdallah ruled with great cruelty.
claims.note: The chroniclers describe harsh punishments and heavy demands for money, especially on Fez. They mostly tell the story from the side of his enemies in the town.

claims.text: Bab Mansour was finished under Abdallah in 1732.
claims.note: Histories of Meknes date the gate, begun under Ismail, to 1732. It is named after its designer, Mansour al-'Alj, a Christian convert to Islam.

reigns.hook: Abdallah is hiding in the deep south. In Meknes the Black Guard need a new sultan, and they reach for another of Ismail's sons: Ali.

images.caption: Frontispiece of an 1890 edition of Thomas Pellow's tale of captivity in Morocco. How true to life it is, nobody knows.
images.alt: Old book illustration of Sultan Moulay Abdallah

reigns.tagline: The soldiers' sultan, until the money ran out
reigns.previously: The Black Guard turn on Abdallah, who flees south to his mother's kin.
paragraphs: Ali was another son of Moulay Ismail, put on the throne by the Black Guard in September 1734 after Abdallah ran for his life. Some later writers call him al-A'raj, "the Lame". He owed his crown entirely to the soldiers, and the soldiers wanted one thing from him: their pay.

He could not find it. Within eighteen months the Black Guard decided that Abdallah, harsh as he was, had been the better bet. On 14 February 1736 they deposed Ali and sent for his brother to come back. Ali did not have long to brood on it. He died in April 1737.

claims.text: Ali was nicknamed al-A'raj, "the Lame".
claims.note: The name turns up in some later histories and lists. Nothing is recorded about how he came by it.

claims.text: The Black Guard dropped him because he could not pay them.
claims.note: The chronicles blame unpaid wages. With so few sources for these years, the full story of the switch back to Abdallah is unclear.

reigns.hook: The soldiers send for Abdallah. He comes back from the south, but the men who recalled him have not forgotten why they threw him out.

reigns.tagline: Back on the throne, and out again by summer
reigns.previously: Ali can't pay the soldiers, so they throw him out.
paragraphs: In 1736 Abdallah came back from exile, called in by the same soldiers who had plotted to kill him less than two years before. He had sat out Ali's reign at Oued Noun, among his mother's kin, the M'gharfa, with his sons around him. One of them, Mohammed, would one day bring this whole mess to an end.

For now, nothing had changed. Abdallah did not trust the soldiers, the soldiers did not trust him, and there was still no money to keep them sweet. His second spell lasted less than six months. On 8 August 1736 the Black Guard deposed him again and went looking for yet another son of Ismail.

claims.text: Abdallah's second reign began on 14 February 1736.
claims.note: Standard lists give 14 February. His biography also gives 23 May 1736, which may be when he was formally proclaimed.

claims.text: He waited out his exile among his mother's people, the M'gharfa of Oued Noun.
claims.note: Khanatha bint Bakkar came from the M'gharfa of the far south, and the chronicles place Abdallah's refuge with his maternal uncles there.

reigns.hook: Abdallah is out once more. The Black Guard's new man is Mohammed, a son of Ismail known by his mother's name, Arbiya. He is about to inherit a hungry country.

images.caption: Detail of Bab Mansour in Meknes, the great gate Abdallah finished in 1732, during his first reign.

reigns.tagline: A hungry country, a fickle army, two years on top
reigns.previously: Abdallah lasts six months before the soldiers depose him again.
paragraphs: Mohammed was one more son of Moulay Ismail, about 42 when the Black Guard raised him in August 1736. People called him Mohammed ben Arbiya, after his mother, to tell him apart from the other Mohammeds in a very large family. He was the soldiers' man from the start, and everyone knew it.

His timing was terrible. The chroniclers tell of drought and famine in the late 1730s, with people going hungry while rival armies tramped across the countryside. A sultan who could neither feed his people nor pay his men had nothing to offer. On 18 June 1738 the Black Guard deposed him. He died the following year.

claims.text: A severe famine struck Morocco during his reign.
claims.note: The chronicles describe drought and hunger in the late 1730s. Exactly which years were worst is not agreed.

claims.text: He was known as Mohammed ben Arbiya, after his mother.
claims.note: Moroccan chronicles name him this way, but his reign is thinly documented and nothing is known of Arbiya herself.

reigns.hook: Mohammed ben Arbiya is gone. The soldiers try yet another brother, al-Mostadi. Abdallah, meanwhile, is out there, waiting for his moment.

reigns.tagline: The brother who would not stay beaten
reigns.previously: Famine bites, and the Black Guard depose Mohammed ben Arbiya.
paragraphs: Al-Mostadi, another son of Moulay Ismail, took the throne when Mohammed ben Arbiya fell in June 1738. He was the sixth of Ismail's sons to be sultan in eleven years, and he did not last much longer than the others. The soldiers who had raised him turned on him, and in February 1740 he was deposed.

Ali and Mohammed ben Arbiya both died soon after losing the throne. Al-Mostadi did not fade away. He became Abdallah's most stubborn rival, rising in revolt again and again, and the throne would come back to him twice more before he was done. He outlived Abdallah, dying in 1759 or 1760.

claims.text: Al-Mostadi kept fighting Abdallah for the throne for most of a decade.
claims.note: The standard lists show him back on the throne in 1742 to 1743 and again in 1747 to 1748, between Abdallah's spells.

claims.text: He died in 1759.
claims.note: The standard list of rulers gives 1759; other references give 1760, and the Hijri year sometimes quoted (1164, that is 1750-51) matches neither.

reigns.hook: Al-Mostadi is out. Abdallah, the sultan who never stays gone, is coming back for a third time. And al-Mostadi has no intention of letting him keep it.

reigns.tagline: Third time on the throne, and still nobody is safe
reigns.previously: The soldiers turn on al-Mostadi and throw him out.
paragraphs: Moulay Abdallah was sultan again, for the third time. After his first fall in 1734 he had run for his life to the far south, to his mother's family in the Oued Noun. In 1736 he got six months back on the throne before losing it again. Through all of it his mother, Khanatha bint Bakkar, Ismail's learned and canny widow, kept working for him.

He came back to a wreck of a country. The soldiers went unpaid and helped themselves instead. Famine had hit hard at the end of the 1730s. And Fez, the great old city, had never warmed to him: at his first proclamation in 1729 he had turned back at the gates and taken the oath in Fes Jdid, the palace quarter, instead.
It lasted sixteen months. On 13 June 1741 the soldiers dropped him once more.

claims.text: After his first fall Abdallah hid among his mother's people in the far south.
claims.note: Al-Nasiri's chronicle says he fled to his maternal uncles in the Oued Noun with his sons, the young Mohammed among them.

claims.text: He snubbed Fez in 1729 because a man in his escort slandered the townspeople.
claims.note: The story comes from al-Nasiri's 19th-century chronicle. It explains the bad blood, but nobody else tells it.

reigns.hook: The soldiers have a new favourite: Zin al-Abidin, yet another of Ismail's many sons. Can he keep them paid where his brother could not?

images.caption: No portrait of Abdallah from his lifetime is known. This photo of about 1920 shows the gate of Dar Dbibegh, the walled palace he built outside Fez in 1729.

reigns.tagline: Five months as sultan, then a quiet twenty years
reigns.previously: The soldiers drop Abdallah for the third time.
paragraphs: Zin al-Abidin was one more of Moulay Ismail's hundreds of children, and by 1741 he was about 49. The Black Guard, the slave army his father built, now picked sultans the way other armies picked camp sites. They wanted their pay, and every new sultan meant fresh handouts.

He could not keep them happy for long. After five months, on 24 November 1741, they threw him out and called Abdallah back. Unlike Abd al-Malik, who was strangled in prison in 1729, Zin al-Abidin was allowed to live. He faded from the story and died around 1762, outliving the brother who replaced him.

claims.text: The Black Guard put the throne up for whoever could pay them.
claims.note: Moroccan chroniclers describe the soldiers making and breaking sultans for money. Historians see a messier contest between the army, Fez and the tribes.

claims.text: Zin al-Abidin lived on for about twenty years after losing the throne.
claims.note: Standard lists give his life as about 1692 to 1762, but the dates are approximate and little else is recorded about him.

reigns.hook: Abdallah is back for a fourth go. Enjoy it while it lasts: this time he will hold the throne for just ten weeks.

reigns.tagline: Ten weeks on the throne, then out the door again
reigns.previously: Zin al-Abidin lasts five months before the soldiers drop him.
paragraphs: Abdallah's fourth spell as sultan was his shortest: about ten weeks, from late November 1741 to early February 1742. There was barely time to unpack. By now the pattern was clear. The soldiers raised a sultan, waited for the money, and dumped him when it ran dry.

Somewhere in all this chaos he found time to build. In Fes Jdid, the royal quarter of Fez, he founded a mosque that still carries his name. His mother and, in the end, he himself would be buried in the royal cemetery beside it. On 3 February 1742 he was out again, and an old rival was back in.

claims.text: Abdallah's fourth spell, about ten weeks long, was the shortest of his six.
claims.note: The standard lists date it from 24 November 1741 to 3 February 1742.

claims.text: He built the Moulay Abdallah Mosque in Fes Jdid, where he is buried.
claims.note: Histories of Fez credit the mosque to him, and he is buried in its necropolis. The year it was built is not recorded.

reigns.hook: Al-Mostadi, thrown out in 1740, wants his throne back. And the soldiers are happy to hand it over.

reigns.tagline: Round two for the brother who would not go away
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne back from Abdallah
reigns.previously: Abdallah's fourth spell is over in ten weeks.
paragraphs: Al-Mostadi had first been sultan in 1738, until the soldiers turned on him in 1740. He never accepted it. Again and again he rose against his brother Abdallah, and in February 1742 he was back on the throne. His birth year is not recorded; he was one of Ismail's many sons, raised in the shadow of a giant.

The country he took over was worn out. Meknes, Ismail's grand capital, was being stripped bare, its palaces falling to pieces. Rival governors and tribes ran their own corners of the kingdom. Al-Mostadi held on for about fifteen months. In May 1743 he was pushed out and Abdallah, of course, came back.

claims.text: Al-Mostadi kept rising against Abdallah, again and again.
claims.note: Moroccan chronicles and later reference works agree he revolted against his brother several times between 1738 and 1748.

claims.text: Ismail's palaces in Meknes were looted and left to crumble during the anarchy.
claims.note: Described by the chroniclers and visible in the ruins. Later sultans also moved materials from Meknes to other cities.

reigns.hook: Abdallah is back for a fifth time, and this spell will last four years. Behind him stands a grown son, Mohammed, who is starting to make his own name.

images.caption: No portrait of al-Mostadi exists. This is the main eastern gate of the royal palace in Meknes, the city his father built up.

reigns.tagline: Four steady years, by the anarchy's standards
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne back from al-Mostadi
reigns.previously: Al-Mostadi loses the throne for the second time.
paragraphs: Abdallah's fifth spell was his longest yet: four years. That counted as stability in those days. He was about 49, hardened by a lifetime of being thrown out and called back.

His smartest move was to give his son Sidi Mohammed Marrakesh to govern. Away from the soldiers in Meknes and the grumbling of Fez, Mohammed learned how to run a country: how to handle the tribes, raise taxes and deal with merchants. He was building the base that would one day carry him to the throne.
In July 1747 the soldiers turned on Abdallah one more time and brought back al-Mostadi.

claims.text: Abdallah made his son Mohammed governor of Marrakesh in the mid-1740s.
claims.note: His years running Marrakesh for his father are well attested, but the start date is not: some references put it in the mid-1740s, others around 1750.

claims.text: Mohammed's time in Marrakesh was his training for the throne.
claims.note: The usual view in histories of the dynasty: he built the skills and support there that he later used as sultan.

reigns.hook: The soldiers have switched sides again. Al-Mostadi is back for a third go. Will it stick this time?

reigns.tagline: Third time on the throne, and the last
reigns.cameToPower: Recalled to the throne a third time
reigns.previously: The soldiers dump Abdallah for the fifth time.
paragraphs: Al-Mostadi got his third turn on the throne in July 1747. Only Abdallah had more. But the old game was running out of road. The Black Guard was not the force it had been in Ismail's day, and the rest of the country was tired of sultans who came and went with the seasons.

After about fifteen months, in October 1748, al-Mostadi was out for good. He never ruled again. He lived on for about another decade, but the throne was settled now. The anarchy had one last act, and it belonged to Abdallah.

claims.text: Al-Mostadi was sultan three separate times.
claims.note: The standard lists show three spells: 1738 to 1740, 1742 to 1743 and 1747 to 1748.

claims.text: He died in 1759.
claims.note: The standard list of rulers gives 1759; other references give 1760, and the Hijri year sometimes quoted (1164, that is 1750-51) matches neither.

reigns.hook: Abdallah is back for the sixth and last time. The soldiers are spent, and this time he will die a sultan.

reigns.tagline: Sixth time lucky: the sultan who outlasted the chaos
reigns.reignEnded: Died at his palace near Fez
reigns.previously: Al-Mostadi falls for the third and last time.
paragraphs: The sixth time was the charm. Abdallah held the throne for nine years, and nobody threw him out. The Black Guard had lost its bite, and his son Mohammed ran much of the country from Marrakesh. In 1754 his mother Khanatha, who had backed him through every fall, died and was buried at his mosque in Fez.
On 1 November 1755 the great earthquake that flattened Lisbon also hit Morocco. Buildings came down in Meknes and Fez, and towns along the coast were battered.

Abdallah died on 10 November 1757 at Dar Dbibegh, the palace he had built outside Fez, and was buried in his mosque in Fes Jdid. He had few sons, and that made all the difference. For once there was no fight.

claims.text: The 1755 Lisbon earthquake did heavy damage in Morocco too.
claims.note: Contemporary reports describe damage in Meknes, Fez and coastal towns. How many died in Morocco is unknown.

claims.text: Abdallah's death brought the smoothest handover since the Saadian Ahmad al-Mansur died in 1603.
claims.note: A common verdict, since he left few rival sons. It depends on how you count earlier, briefly contested successions.

reigns.hook: Thirty years of chaos end with a funeral. Sidi Mohammed, seasoned by years in Marrakesh, takes the throne and sets out to tame the army that broke his father.

reigns.tagline: The sultan who said hello to the United States
reigns.reignEnded: Died after 32 years on the throne
reigns.previously: Abdallah dies after six spells as sultan. The anarchy is over.
paragraphs: Sidi Mohammed took over a broken country and fixed it. He brought the Black Guard to heel and got the country working again. When the great earthquake of 1755, the one that flattened Lisbon, left Moroccan towns in ruins, he rebuilt. In the 1760s he founded a whole new port, Essaouira (the Europeans called it Mogador), laid out by a French engineer, and steered foreign trade through it so he could tax it.

In 1769 he took Mazagan, today El Jadida, the last Portuguese fortress on the Atlantic coast. And on 20 December 1777 he opened his ports to American ships, at a time when the United States was still fighting for its independence. In 1786 the two countries signed a treaty of friendship that is still in force.
He was always busy with trade, treaties and reform. But his son al-Yazid was a constant headache, rebelling and hiding in shrines. When Mohammed died in April 1790, Yazid was ready.

claims.text: Morocco was the first country to recognise the United States.
claims.note: Both governments tell it this way, pointing to the 1777 declaration. Historians note it was an opening of ports, not a formal act of recognition.

claims.text: The 1786 treaty with Morocco is the oldest unbroken treaty in US history.
claims.note: Renegotiated in 1836 and still in force; it is counted as the longest unbroken treaty relationship in US history.

claims.text: Abdallah Laroui called him 'the architect of modern Morocco'.
claims.note: The Moroccan historian's verdict on his reforms of the army, trade and government.

reigns.hook: The careful sultan is gone. His wild son al-Yazid, years in disgrace, grabs the throne and starts settling old scores.

reigns.tagline: Two years of revenge, ended on the battlefield
reigns.previously: Mohammed III dies. His disgraced son al-Yazid is ready to pounce.
paragraphs: Moulay al-Yazid had spent years at war with his own father, rebelling, sulking in sanctuary at holy shrines and bouncing between disgrace and pardon. When Mohammed III died in 1790, Yazid grabbed the throne and set about punishing everyone who had crossed him.

The Jews of Tétouan had once refused him money. Now he let his troops loose on them: homes were looted and people were killed. European witnesses, among them the English surgeon William Lempriere, described the violence. He also went to war with Spain and sent his army against Ceuta in 1790 and 1791.

His brutality cost him support fast, and brothers were proclaimed sultan in other cities. In February 1792 he fought the backers of his brother Hisham near Marrakesh, was badly wounded, and died on 23 February.

claims.text: Al-Yazid took violent revenge on the Jews of Tétouan for refusing him money.
claims.note: Recorded in contemporary accounts, including that of William Lempriere, who was in Morocco at the time.

claims.text: Rival brothers were proclaimed sultan in other cities while al-Yazid still reigned.
claims.note: The chronicles record Hisham's proclamation in Marrakesh and other claims in the south before Yazid's death.

reigns.hook: Yazid is dead and Morocco has too many sultans. Hisham holds Marrakesh, and in Fez the scholars hail another brother, the bookish Slimane.

reigns.previously: Sultan Yazid dies of a wound, and his brothers split the country.
paragraphs: After Sultan Yazid died in 1792, Morocco split. Hisham was proclaimed sultan in Marrakesh and the south, while his brother Slimane held Fez and the north.
Plague and Slimane's advances wore Hisham down, and by 1797 he had given up and submitted.
reigns.hook: Slimane rules a reunited Morocco.

reigns.tagline: The scholar sultan who shut the door on Europe
reigns.previously: Al-Yazid dies of battle wounds. His brothers are proclaimed sultan.
paragraphs: Moulay Slimane (also spelled Sulayman) was a scholar first and a sultan second. The religious elite of Fez proclaimed him soon after Yazid died, but he had to share Morocco with his brother Hisham in Marrakesh until 1797. Then a terrible plague in 1799 and 1800 killed vast numbers of people.

He was pious and strict, and he wanted Morocco left alone. He cut back trade with Europe, and in about 1817 and 1818 he shut down the old state-backed corsair raids on foreign shipping. Napoleon's wars raged across the strait and he kept well out of them.

His last years were hard. Berber tribes of the Middle Atlas beat his army and briefly took him prisoner. When it came to the succession he passed over his own sons and named his nephew Abd al-Rahman. He died in Marrakesh in November 1822.

claims.text: Slimane was won over by the strict reformist ideas of the Wahhabis of Arabia.
claims.note: He did attack some popular Sufi practices. Historians argue over how far that was Wahhabi influence or his own Moroccan scholarly tradition.

claims.text: Berber rebels captured the sultan himself after beating his army.
claims.note: The chronicles report it, but the details of the battle and his captivity differ between them.

claims.text: He picked his nephew over his own sons as heir.
claims.note: Abd al-Rahman, son of his brother Hisham, succeeded him as Slimane had chosen.

reigns.hook: The nephew takes the throne. Eight years later, across the border, a French army lands in Algiers, and Morocco's quiet isolation is over.

images.caption: The Moulay Slimane Mosque in Rabat, which he built in 1812. No reliable portrait of him survives.

reigns.tagline: He backed the wrong horse against France and paid for it
reigns.previously: Slimane dies, skipping his sons to name his nephew as heir.
paragraphs: Moulay Abd al-Rahman reigned for 37 years, and most of them were shaped by one event: in 1830 France invaded Algeria next door. When the Algerian resistance leader Emir Abd al-Qadir fought back, Morocco gave him shelter and support. In 1832 a French mission came to the sultan at Meknes. A young painter called Eugène Delacroix came along and sketched everything he saw.

France lost patience in 1844. Its navy shelled Tangier and Mogador, and on 14 August, at the river Isly near Oujda, Marshal Bugeaud's army routed a much bigger Moroccan force led by the sultan's son Muhammad. The Treaty of Tangier that followed made Morocco drop Abd al-Qadir.
It was a humiliation, but Abd al-Rahman held on to his country's independence and its land. He died in Meknes in August 1859, aged 81. The son who had lost at Isly took over.

claims.text: The French bombarded Tangier and Mogador as well as beating the Moroccan army at Isly.
claims.note: The 1844 naval attacks and the battle are well recorded on both sides.

claims.text: Delacroix saw the sultan in person and sketched him.
claims.note: Delacroix was with the Comte de Mornay's mission in 1832. He painted the big canvas in 1845 from his notes and sketches.

reigns.hook: Mohammed, the son beaten at Isly, takes the throne. Within weeks Spain declares war, and its army marches on Tétouan.

reigns.tagline: A lost war, a giant bill and the creditors at the door
reigns.previously: Abd al-Rahman dies, having kept Morocco independent but humbled.
paragraphs: Sidi Mohammed had led Morocco's army to defeat at Isly, so he knew what European guns could do. He had barely taken the throne when Spain declared war over tribal raids on its enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla. Spanish troops pushed down the coast and took Tétouan in February 1860.

The peace of Wad Ras in 1860 hit hard. Morocco had to pay a huge war indemnity, and Spain kept Tétouan until the money was paid in 1862. To find the cash the sultan borrowed from Britain and handed half his customs duties to Spain, so Europeans now had a hand in Morocco's purse.
He tried to catch up by training a new army on European lines. He died in Marrakesh in September 1873, with the job far from done.

claims.text: The Wad Ras indemnity was about twenty times the Moroccan government's yearly budget.
claims.note: A widely quoted figure, including on Wikipedia. Moroccan state revenues of the time are hard to pin down, so treat it as a rough scale.

claims.text: Half of Morocco's customs duties went to paying off Spain.
claims.note: Half the duties at Moroccan ports were set aside for the Spanish debt; part of the indemnity was paid with money lent by Britain.

reigns.hook: His son Hassan, a soldier sultan, inherits a country ringed by European creditors. He means to hold it together from the saddle.

reigns.tagline: The sultan who ruled from the saddle
reigns.previously: Mohammed IV dies, leaving a sultanate deep in debt to Europe.
paragraphs: Hassan I hardly ever sat still. Most years, from spring to autumn, he took the whole court on the road: ministers, treasury, thousands of troops. Tribes that paid their taxes and swore loyalty got off lightly. Tribes that didn't got a visit from the army. He marched to the Sous, into the Rif and, in 1893, across the High Atlas to Tafilalt, the oasis his family came from.

He knew Morocco had to modernise or be swallowed. France took Tunisia in 1881 and Britain occupied Egypt in 1882. Hassan hired foreign officers to drill his soldiers, sent students to Europe, built an arms works in Fez and struck new coins. He played Britain, France and Spain off against each other. At the Madrid Conference of 1880 he tried to curb the foreign 'protection' that let Moroccans dodge his courts and taxes, and came away with little.

In June 1894 he fell ill and died on campaign in the Tadla region, deep in hostile country. His chamberlain, Ba Ahmed, kept it quiet. The sultan's litter travelled on, curtains closed, until the army reached safety. Only then did the news break, along with the name of the new sultan: Hassan's young son Abdelaziz.

claims.text: Hassan took the court and army on campaign almost every year of his reign.
claims.note: Court letters and European visitors describe the yearly expeditions; historians such as Pennell and Miller treat this as the core of his rule.

claims.text: His throne was his saddle.
claims.note: A later saying that sums up his reign. Nobody at the time is recorded saying it.

claims.text: Ba Ahmed hid the sultan's death, carrying the body in a closed litter as if he were alive.
claims.note: The secrecy is well attested. The details of the litter come from the standard retellings and vary a little.

reigns.hook: Ba Ahmed has moved fast. Hassan's teenage son Abdelaziz is proclaimed sultan, and the chamberlain who hid the body will rule in his name.

reigns.tagline: The boy sultan who fell for bicycles and cameras
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir, installed by Ba Ahmed
reigns.previously: Hassan I dies on campaign, and his chamberlain hides the body.
paragraphs: Abdelaziz was a boy when he became sultan, and for six years the real ruler was Ba Ahmed, the old chamberlain. When Ba Ahmed died in 1900, the young sultan took charge and threw the palace open to Europe. Bicycles, cameras, fireworks, gadgets, a golden state coach: if it was new and foreign, he wanted it. European salesmen and advisers crowded his court, and many Moroccans were scandalised.

He tried real reform too, with a new tax on farmland and livestock that everyone would pay. It was badly run, the money dried up, and he borrowed from French banks. In 1905 Kaiser Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to challenge France, and the crisis ended at the Algeciras Conference of 1906, which put Morocco's customs, police and finances under international supervision.

In 1907 France occupied Oujda. That summer, after European workers were killed in Casablanca, French warships shelled the town and troops landed; French reports gave 600 to 1,500 Moroccan dead; other estimates go as high as 7,000. In August his brother Abdelhafid was proclaimed sultan in Marrakesh. A year later Abdelaziz's army fell apart near the city and he gave up. He retired to Tangier and lived there until 1943.

claims.text: Abdelaziz sold Morocco for a bicycle.
claims.note: A jibe from his critics. The spending was real, but the debts and the loss of independence came from much bigger forces.

claims.text: His palace filled with European novelties, from bicycles and cameras to a golden state coach.
claims.note: Described by European visitors and journalists at the time, though some of them played it up for laughs.

reigns.hook: Abdelhafid has won the throne by promising holy war on the Europeans. Now he has to deal with them, and pay their bills.

reigns.tagline: The holy warrior who signed Morocco away
reigns.cameToPower: Won a civil war against his brother
reigns.previously: Abdelaziz's army collapses near Marrakesh, and he gives up the throne.
paragraphs: Abdelhafid was everything his brother wasn't: a scholar, a poet and a tough governor of Marrakesh. The great lords of the south, led by the Glaoui family, backed him, and he took the throne promising to throw out the Europeans and tear up their treaties. Once in power, he found he couldn't. The powers would only recognise him if he accepted Algeciras and his brother's debts. He gave in.

His rule turned harsh. Rivals and critics were tortured or killed. In 1911 rebel tribes besieged him in Fez and he begged France for help. French troops marched in. Germany sent a gunboat to Agadir in protest, and a deal between the two powers left France free to take Morocco.

On 30 March 1912 Abdelhafid signed the Treaty of Fez. Morocco became a French protectorate, Spain got a zone in the north, and Tangier later became an international zone. Weeks later Moroccan troops in Fez mutinied and killed their French officers, and the city rioted. In August Abdelhafid abdicated and sailed for France. He died near Paris in 1937.

claims.text: Abdelhafid had the captured rebel Bu Hmara thrown to his lions.
claims.note: Reported by Europeans in Fez in 1909. Versions differ on what the lions did and on how Bu Hmara finally died.

claims.text: The Treaty of Fez made Morocco a French protectorate.
claims.note: Signed on 30 March 1912; a Franco-Spanish treaty that November set out Spain's zone.

claims.text: He was paid a large pension to step down.
claims.note: He bargained hard with the French over the terms, which later Moroccan nationalists held against him.

reigns.hook: The French need a sultan who won't make trouble. They pick Abdelhafid's quiet half-brother Yusef.

reigns.tagline: The sultan who reigned while Lyautey ruled
reigns.previously: Abdelhafid signs Morocco over to France, then abdicates.
paragraphs: Yusef was a quiet man with no public profile, and that was the point. Real power lay with the French resident-general, Hubert Lyautey. Lyautey loved the old Morocco and kept up its ceremony: the sultan prayed, presided and signed decrees. Beside the old medinas the French built new European towns with wide boulevards, and Rabat became the capital.

In the Spanish zone, a Rif judge and journalist named Abd el-Krim led the mountain tribes in revolt. At Annual in July 1921 his men wiped out a Spanish army; the Spanish dead are put at anywhere from about 8,000 to over 10,000. He declared a Republic of the Rif. In 1925 he struck into the French zone, and France and Spain hit back together, with Marshal Pétain leading the French. Abd el-Krim surrendered in 1926.
Yusef died suddenly in Fez in November 1927. He had older sons, but the French had their own ideas about who would make a good sultan.

claims.text: Lyautey ran Morocco while the sultan reigned in name.
claims.note: Under the protectorate the resident-general held real authority; historians agree Yusef had little say in policy.

claims.text: More than 10,000 Spanish soldiers died at Annual.
claims.note: Estimates run from about 8,000 to over 10,000, depending on how the whole retreat is counted.

reigns.hook: The French pass over Yusef's older sons and choose the youngest, Mohammed, aged 18. They think he will be easy to handle.

reigns.tagline: The shy teenager who became the face of independence
reigns.previously: Sultan Yusef dies, and the French choose his youngest son.
paragraphs: The French chose Mohammed because he was young and shy. In 1930 he signed the 'Berber dahir', which moved Berber areas out from under Islamic law and into customary courts. Young Moroccans saw a plot to split Arabs from Berbers, and protests filled the mosques. A nationalist movement was born, and slowly the sultan drifted towards it.

In the Second World War, Vichy France ran Morocco until the Allies landed in November 1942. In January 1943 Roosevelt dined with the sultan at the Anfa conference in Casablanca. In 1944 the Istiqlal (Independence) Party demanded freedom outright, and in a speech at Tangier in 1947 the sultan backed it. On 20 August 1953 France deposed him and sent him into exile, first to Corsica, then to Madagascar.

Morocco erupted in bombings, riots and armed revolt, and France gave way. On 16 November 1955 he came home to vast, cheering crowds. France recognised independence on 2 March 1956, and Spain gave up its northern zone that April. In 1957 he took the title of king. In February 1961, aged 51, he died after a minor operation, and his son Hassan took over.

claims.text: Mohammed V shielded Morocco's Jews from Vichy's anti-Jewish laws.
claims.note: He is widely honoured for it and resisted some measures, but Vichy decrees were partly applied in Morocco under his seal. Historians argue over how much he could and did do.

claims.text: The French picked him at 18 because they thought he would be docile.
claims.note: The usual account, drawn from how the choice looked at the time; the French officials' own reasoning is less clearly recorded.

claims.text: He met President Roosevelt at the Anfa conference in January 1943.
claims.note: Recorded by American and Moroccan witnesses, including his son Hassan, who was there.

reigns.hook: Rewind to August 1953. The French are tired of a sultan who backs independence. They fly him into exile and crown an elderly relative instead.

reigns.tagline: The sultan France made and Morocco never accepted
reigns.cameToPower: Installed by the French and El Glaoui
reigns.previously: August 1953: France deposes Mohammed V and sends him into exile.
paragraphs: Mohammed Ben Aarafa was a quiet, elderly member of the royal family, a grandson of Sultan Mohammed IV, with no following of his own. That suited the French. On 21 August 1953, the day after they exiled Mohammed V, they put him on the throne, cheered on by Thami El Glaoui, the mighty pasha of Marrakesh. Most Moroccans refused to accept him, and the Spanish zone ignored him altogether.

On 11 September 1953, less than a month in, a nationalist named Allal ben Abdallah attacked him with a knife in Rabat and was shot dead. Bombings and riots spread, and armed bands took to the hills. By 1955 even the Glaoui had turned against him. On 1 October 1955 Ben Aarafa left for Tangier, and his abdication followed that month. He spent the rest of his life abroad and died in Nice in 1976.

claims.text: Allal ben Abdallah attacked Ben Aarafa with a knife and was shot dead.
claims.note: Reported at the time and remembered in Morocco, where Allal ben Abdallah is honoured as a martyr of independence.

claims.text: The Moroccan state does not count Ben Aarafa as a sultan.
claims.note: Official lists of the dynasty leave him out, and his reign was never recognised in the Spanish zone.

reigns.hook: Back to the main story: in November 1955 Mohammed V flies home to a hero's welcome. When he dies in 1961, his son Hassan, 31, takes the throne.

reigns.tagline: The survivor king of the Years of Lead
reigns.previously: Mohammed V dies after minor surgery; his son Hassan takes over.
paragraphs: Hassan was clever, charming and hard. He gave Morocco its first constitution in 1962 but kept the real power. In 1965 riots in Casablanca were crushed and he declared a state of emergency that lasted until 1970. That October his fiercest critic, the opposition leader Mehdi Ben Barka, was seized on a Paris street and never seen again. Then the army turned on him, twice.

On 10 July 1971, at his birthday party at the Skhirat palace, mutinous cadets burst in shooting. About 100 guests were killed, and nearly 280 people died that day in all. On 16 August 1972 air force jets fired on his airliner as he flew home from Europe. It landed safely. His defence minister, General Mohamed Oufkir, was blamed and died that night. Oufkir's wife and six children were then held in secret prisons for about 15 years.

The Years of Lead followed: arrests, torture, disappearances and secret jails such as Tazmamart, where many of the coup soldiers died. In 1975 his Green March sent about 350,000 unarmed Moroccans into Spanish Sahara. Morocco calls it its southern provinces; the Algerian-backed Polisario Front fought for independence until a UN ceasefire in 1991, and the UN lists it as non-self-governing. He eased his grip in the 1990s, and in 1998 an opposition leader became prime minister.

claims.text: Hassan saved himself in 1972 by grabbing the radio and posing as a mechanic who said the king was badly hurt.
claims.note: Widely told, and it comes from the king's own circle. Other versions give him different words, and the pilots' side of it is unclear.

claims.text: General Oufkir shot himself after the 1972 plot failed.
claims.note: Suicide was the official verdict, but he was found with several bullet wounds, and his family says he was executed.

claims.text: Hassan's state ran secret prisons where prisoners were tortured and many died.
claims.note: Told by survivors and human rights groups, and acknowledged by Morocco's own Equity and Reconciliation Commission in 2005.

reigns.hook: Hassan dies in July 1999 after 38 years on the throne. His son Mohammed, 35, inherits the crown and a country hoping for change.

reigns.tagline: The latest king of a dynasty older than the United States
reigns.previously: Hassan II dies after 38 years; his son Mohammed is king.
paragraphs: Mohammed VI came to the throne at 35 and moved quickly to mark a change. He dismissed Driss Basri, his father's long-serving interior minister. In May 2003 suicide bombers struck Casablanca, killing more than 40 people. In 2004 a new family code, the Moudawana, raised the marriage age for women to 18 and gave wives more rights. A truth commission looked into the abuses of his father's reign and reported in 2005.

In 2011, as the Arab Spring swept the region, the 20 February movement marched for reform. The king offered a new constitution, approved by referendum that July, which gave the elected head of government more power and made Amazigh (Berber) an official language. Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, and in December 2020 the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as Morocco restored ties with Israel; Polisario and Algeria reject the claim.

In September 2023 the Al Haouz earthquake killed nearly 3,000 people in the High Atlas. Morocco's footballers reached the 2022 World Cup semi-final, and the country will co-host the 2030 World Cup. After the September 2026 election he named Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri the first woman head of government. The Alaouites have ruled since the 1660s, and the heir, Crown Prince Moulay Hassan, was born in 2003.

claims.text: The Equity and Reconciliation Commission was the Arab world's first truth commission.
claims.note: Set up in 2004 to examine abuses under Hassan II; its 2005 report acknowledged deaths and disappearances but named no perpetrators.

claims.text: In December 2020 the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.
claims.note: Announced alongside Morocco's renewed ties with Israel. Morocco regards the territory as its southern provinces; the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, rejects this and seeks independence; the UN lists it as non-self-governing.

claims.text: The 2011 constitution made Amazigh an official language alongside Arabic.
claims.note: Approved by referendum on 1 July 2011.
